title: Truth, fiercely
hook: the Kotzker rebbe demanded truth without comfort

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebbe Nachman's turn: if you believe you can damage, believe you can repair. Your line was you can repair. What did you mend, and is it done? Day one thousand two hundred one.

These last days have been warm ones. Joy that opens. A rebbe at the head of the table. Pulling sadness into the dance. Today the temperature drops. In the small Polish town of Kotzk lived a Hasidic rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel, who had little patience for warmth that wasn't real. Stories about him are sharp, short, and a little frightening. Tradition says he would rather have a handful of followers who were honest than crowds who were comfortable. His whole life circled one word, and he wanted it without any padding. Today's word.
screen: `THE TEMPERATURE DROPS.` → `A REBBE IN KOTZK.` → `NO PADDING.`

segments.voice: Truth. In Hebrew, emet. First, the Bible's standard. The psalm asks who may dwell on God's holy mountain, and part of its answer is the one who "speaketh truth in his heart." Not only with the mouth. In the heart, where nobody checks. Second, the sages. The Talmud teaches that God's seal is truth. And it notices something about the word itself: emet is spelled with the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a letter from the middle, and the last. Truth, the sages suggest, runs the whole length, beginning to end. Third, the Kotzker. Sayings attributed to him are passed on by his followers, and one of them goes like this: everything in the world can be imitated except truth, because truth that's imitated isn't truth anymore. He aimed it first at religious life. Prayer done for show, piety performed for the neighbors, a warm feeling worn like a coat. To him, those were imitations, and he'd take an honest struggle over a comfortable fake. Fourth, the cost, said fairly. The Kotzker's way is hard, and Hasidic tradition itself remembers him as a fierce and solitary figure. Not every teacher walked his road, and the other Hasidic teachers we've met lean toward warmth and joy. His question can sit underneath the warm paths too. Is this real? Am I telling the truth in my heart, where nobody checks? That's what fiercely means here. Not cruelty to others. Honesty with yourself, without padding.
screen: `SPEAKETH TRUTH IN HIS HEART.` · `FIRST, MIDDLE AND LAST.` · `TRUTH CAN'T BE IMITATED.` · `HONEST WITH YOURSELF, NO PADDING.` · then, large: `TRUTH, FIERCELY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about one thing. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself one plain question and let the answer come without dressing it up. What am I pretending about? Maybe it's a feeling you claim not to have. A habit you call fine. A reason you give that isn't the real reason. When the answer comes, don't argue with it, and don't punish yourself for it. Just let it be true for a minute. That's the Kotzker's whole demand: see it as it is. If you pray, you can stand before God with exactly that, and nothing extra. The bell holds the time.
Truth. Emet in Hebrew, God's seal for the sages, and for the Kotzker rebbe the one thing that can't be imitated. Today's word.
Your line: truth, fiercely. Today, once, when you're about to give the polished answer, give the true one instead, kindly and plainly. Day one thousand two hundred one.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching counts honesty, in speech and in the heart, among the basic demands of the Torah; the sayings of the Kotzker rebbe are retold in Hasidic and wider Jewish circles as a challenge to empty piety.
